prompt.context: Massive Dynamic is a multi-national pharmaceutical company. One of their assets, Cortexiphan, is an anti-infective that successfully treats three major types of hospital-born illness and is currently in Phase II clinical trials. Unfortunately, Massive Dynamic only has the capital to finance a Phase III clinical trial for one of the three illnesses that Cortexiphan treats.
prompt.question: Walter Bishop, Chief Medical Officer of Massive Dynamic, has enlisted your help to decide which of the three possible indications for Cortexiphan they should pursue to maximize profits over a five-year period post-launch.

clarifying_info.a: The drug is only likely to be approved in the US at this time.

clarifying_info.q: How will the drug be distributed?
clarifying_info.a: The drug will be sold directly to hospitals by Massive Dynamic; no need to consider distribution channel costs.

clarifying_info.q: Should we use NPV for the financial analysis?
clarifying_info.a: No need to calculate based on NPV; just do total over five years without discounting.

exhibits.title: Market Overview by Indication
exhibits.shows: A table showing three indications (Candidiasis, Rare Molds, Aspergillosis) with competitor market share breakdown, annual dose volumes, and average price per dose.

exhibits.title: Cortexiphan Clinical and Development Profile
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three indications on probability of Phase III trial success, Phase III trial cost, production cost per dose, safety profile vs. market leader, and efficacy profile vs. market leader.

exhibits.title: Cortexiphan Aspergillosis Formulary Status Distribution by Pricing Strategy
exhibits.shows: A table showing how hospitals distribute across formulary status categories (No Restrictions, On Formulary Restricted, Off Formulary) for three pricing strategies (Parity $10, Premium $15, Discount $5), and the expected market share at each formulary status.

framework: Market sizing: calculate total addressable market for each indication (annual doses x avg price)
Competitive landscape: assess number of competitors, market concentration, and likelihood of gaining share
Clinical profile fit: evaluate Cortexiphan's safety and efficacy vs. market leader in each indication
Market share estimation: derive expected share given clinical profile and competitive dynamics
Financial analysis: compute annual profit per indication using (revenue/dose - cost/dose) x expected doses
Risk-adjusted expected profit: weight 5-year profit by probability of Phase III success, net of trial cost
Pricing strategy: evaluate discount vs. parity vs. premium and impact on formulary status and total profit

questions.prompt: What are your initial thoughts on Exhibit 1 — market size and competition for each indication?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total market size for each indication and make qualitative observations about competitive intensity. Aspergillosis: 6 competitors, two with very small share suggesting fragmentation at the low end. Rare Molds: only 2 products, clear market leader at 75%; physicians likely want more options and a lower-cost alternative to $20/dose. Candidiasis: crowded with 5 competitors and no clear leader; penetration will require strong clinical differentiation. Candidate should note that Candidiasis is the largest market but competitive dynamics are challenging.

math.setup: Total market size = Annual Doses x Avg Price per Dose
math.answer: Candidiasis is largest at $25B; Aspergillosis $15B; Rare Molds $4B. More info on development costs and likely market share needed before deciding.

questions.prompt: Given the clinical profile in Exhibit 2, what market share would you expect Cortexiphan to capture in each indication, and what is the annual profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should reason from clinical profile to market share: Aspergillosis — superior efficacy implies new market leader (~50-60%); Rare Molds — equal profile, split with leader, slight disadvantage from not being first to market (~40-50%); Candidiasis — poor safety in a crowded market at same price means very low share (<25% of leader). Interviewer should confirm: Asp=60%, Rare Molds=40%, Candidiasis=10%. Then candidate should calculate annual profit using Profit = (Revenue/dose - Cost/dose) x (Market Share x Total Annual Doses).

math.setup: Annual Profit = (Price per Dose - Production Cost per Dose) x (Market Share x Annual Doses)
math.answer: Aspergillosis generates highest annual profit at $2.7B, followed by Candidiasis at $1.5B and Rare Molds at $1.2B.

questions.prompt: Accounting for the 5-year window, probability of trial success, and trial cost, which indication should be chosen?
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute risk-adjusted expected profit over 5 years. Profit if success = annual profit x 5. Loss if fail = trial cost. Expected Profit = (Prob Success x 5-year profit) - (Prob Fail x trial cost). Aspergillosis dominates on both highest expected profit and highest absolute upside.

math.setup: 5-year Profit if Success = Annual Profit x 5 years; Expected Profit = (P_success x 5yr profit) - (P_fail x trial cost)
steps: Aspergillosis: 5yr profit = $2.7B x 5 = $13.5B; net of trial = $13.5B - $2.0B = $11.5B; Expected = $11.5B x 50% - $2.0B x 50% = $5.75B - $1.0B = $4.75B
Candidiasis: 5yr profit = $1.5B x 5 = $7.5B; net = $7.5B - $1.0B = $6.5B; Expected = $6.5B x 60% - $1.0B x 40% = $3.9B - $0.4B = $3.5B
math.answer: Aspergillosis has highest expected profit at $4.75B; Candidiasis second at $3.5B; Rare Molds last at $1.0B. Aspergillosis should be selected.

questions.prompt: What are the main pros and cons of pricing Cortexiphan at a premium vs. a discount vs. parity for the aspergillosis indication?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming exercise. Strong candidates will cover both strategic and financial dimensions. See brainstorming section for full expected answer.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the overall market share and annual revenue at each price point for the aspergillosis indication. Which pricing strategy maximizes profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute blended market share as sum-product of (% hospitals at formulary status x expected market share at that status), then calculate annual revenue and 5-year profit net of trial cost. Premium pricing wins because higher price per dose more than compensates for lower market share.

math.setup: Blended Market Share = sum over formulary statuses of (% hospitals at status x expected share at status); Annual Revenue = Total Doses x Blended Share x Price; 5-yr Profit = Revenue x 5 - trial cost
steps: Premium 5-yr profit: ($15 - $7) x 0.75B doses/yr x 5 yrs - $2B trial = $30B - $2B = $28B
math.answer: Premium at $15/dose yields $11.25B annual revenue, $28B 5-year profit. This is the highest across all three strategies.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the main pros and cons of pricing Cortexiphan at a premium vs. a discount for the aspergillosis indication?

categories.name: Premium Pricing — Pros
ideas: Signals to market that product is better than current options, consistent with superior clinical profile
Can selectively offer discounts to certain hospitals if needed without proactively sacrificing revenue

categories.name: Premium Pricing — Cons
ideas: Worse formulary status and lower market share
Negative publicity given current media and government pressure on high pharmaceutical prices

categories.name: Discount Pricing — Pros
ideas: Higher market share and quicker product uptake
Can take price increases over time once established

categories.name: Discount Pricing — Cons
ideas: Sets a low price expectation that could hinder pricing for rare molds or candidiasis if pursued later

recommendation: Pursue the aspergillosis indication at a premium price of $15 per dose
This strategy yields expected 5-year revenues of $56.25B and profits of approximately $28B

Aspergillosis is preferred over candidiasis due to Cortexiphan's superior efficacy profile, high expected market share of 60%, and a sizeable market; despite candidiasis being a larger market, the poor safety profile limits share capture
Premium pricing is preferred because the higher price per dose more than offsets the formulary status disadvantage
risks: 50% probability that the Phase III trial fails, resulting in a $2B loss from trial costs
Premium pricing may invite negative publicity and regulatory scrutiny in a politically sensitive drug pricing environment
Formulary restrictions under premium pricing leave 25% of hospitals off-formulary, limiting access
Future indications (rare molds, candidiasis) may face anchoring challenges if premium price sets a different precedent than originally intended
next_steps: Proceed with Phase III clinical trial for the aspergillosis indication
Engage hospital formulary committees early to build relationships and support formulary inclusion
Develop a payer and provider engagement strategy to support premium pricing
Monitor clinical trial progress and prepare commercial launch plan contingent on trial success
